subject: Computer Networking
title: HTTPS and TLS
description: A quick win: understand HTTPS and TLS.

hook.text: HTTP sends everything in plain text. Passwords, card numbers, messages — anyone could read them.

buildup.text: TLS wraps HTTP in encryption. The combination is called HTTPS — the 'S' stands for Secure.

discovery.text: TLS starts with a handshake: the server proves its identity with a certificate signed by a trusted authority.

twist.text: After the handshake, both sides derive a shared secret key. All data flows through that encrypted channel.

climax.text: Modern browsers mark plain HTTP sites as 'Not Secure.' HTTPS is now the baseline, not the exception.

punchline.text: TLS makes HTTP private. That's why the padlock matters.

quiz.question: How does a server prove its identity in TLS?
options: By presenting a certificate signed by a trusted authority
By sending its source code to the client
By sharing its private encryption key

details.summary: HTTPS wraps HTTP inside a TLS encrypted tunnel, protecting data confidentiality, integrity, and server authenticity. TLS uses certificates to verify server identity and asymmetric cryptography to establish a shared secret, then encrypts all traffic with fast symmetric ciphers.
details.whyItMatters: HTTPS is now the baseline for all web communication. Without it, passwords, personal data, and financial information travel in plain text visible to anyone on the network path.
takeaways: TLS encrypts all HTTP traffic between browser and server
Certificates verify the server is who it claims to be
Modern TLS 1.3 completes the handshake in a single round trip

faq.question: How does the TLS handshake work?
faq.answer: The client sends supported cipher suites, the server responds with its certificate and chosen cipher. The client verifies the certificate chain and they exchange key material to derive shared encryption keys. TLS 1.3 completes this in one round trip, while TLS 1.2 requires two.

faq.question: Is HTTPS required for all websites?
faq.answer: Browsers now mark HTTP sites as insecure and may block certain features. Search engines rank HTTPS sites higher. Let's Encrypt provides free certificates, eliminating cost barriers. Every website should use HTTPS, even if it serves only static content, to protect user privacy.
